name: TPS613221ADBVR
title: TPS61322 family: fixed-output synchronous boost converter, 6.5 µA quiescent, up to 1.8 A switch current
summary: A family of tiny synchronous boost converters for one to three alkaline or NiMH cells or one Li-ion cell. Each runs from 0.9 V to 5.5 V in, draws 6.5 µA into VOUT, and boosts to an output fixed inside the chip (2.0 V to 5.0 V across the family; TPS613221A gives 3.3 V). Hysteretic current control with a 200 mA inductor ripple and synchronous rectification needs only an inductor and an output capacitor; an external Schottky diode raises the output current. The parts differ in output voltage and switch current limit, and come in a 3-pin or 5-pin SOT-23.
key_figures: 0.9 V to 5.5 V (runs down to 0.4 V after start-up)
0.75 A min, 1.20 A typ, 1.60 A max
200 mΩ low side, 1000 mΩ high side
0.7 µH to 13 µH / 4.7 µF to 100 µF

notes: TPS61322 comes in the 3-pin DBZ package; the TPS61322xA devices come in the 5-pin DBV package and also have a 3-pin DBZ pin assignment.
Preproduction parts are prototypes not yet released for full production. A part may carry further marking for logo, lot trace or environmental category.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit
circuits.description: The whole converter is the chip, one inductor and one output capacitor. The battery feeds L1, whose other end goes to SW; C1 sits from VOUT to ground and the fixed-voltage output leaves from VOUT.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit without Schottky diode (Figure 8-1)
circuits.description: A 2.2 V supply for a load such as a wireless mouse drawing under 50 mA from one alkaline cell (0.9 V to 1.6 V in, ±10 mV ripple target). A 4.7 µH inductor runs from the cell to SW and 22 µF holds VOUT; the internal synchronous rectifier needs no diode.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit with Schottky diode (Figure 8-9)
circuits.description: A 5.0 V, 500 mA rail of the USB OTG kind from a 3 V to 4.35 V source (±25 mV ripple target). A Schottky D1 from SW to VOUT carries current beside the internal high-side FET, and R1 in series with C2 across D1 snubs the switch node. L1 is 2.2 µH and C1 22 µF.

parts.note: snubber capacitor, typical value; more than three times the diode capacitance

notes: R1 = 5 Ω and C2 = 120 pF are typical values. Figures 8-18 and 8-19 are measured with a ZLLS410TA as D1.

circuits.title: True shutdown for TPS61322xx (Figure 8-20)
circuits.description: A switch Q1 in series with the battery disconnects the converter completely. Behind Q1, C1 (2.2 µF) decouples the input to the 2.2 µH inductor; C2 (22 µF) holds VOUT. Q1 may be mechanical or a P-channel MOSFET or PNP transistor; D1 from SW to VOUT is fitted only for large output current.

circuits.title: True shutdown, V_MCU voltage no less than battery voltage (Figure 8-21)
circuits.description: A P-channel MOSFET Q1 between the battery and the converter's input, switched by an MCU whose supply is at or above the battery voltage. R1 pulls Q1's gate up to the battery so the converter is off; the GPIO drives the gate directly to turn it on. C1 2.2 µF, L1 2.2 µH, C2 22 µF; D1 only for large current.

circuits.title: True shutdown, V_MCU voltage less than battery voltage (Figure 8-22)
circuits.description: The same P-channel cut-off switch for an MCU whose supply sits below the battery. R1 holds Q1's gate at the battery, so Q1 is off; the GPIO drives the gate of N-channel Q2, which pulls Q1's gate to ground and turns the converter's input on. C1 2.2 µF, L1 2.2 µH, C2 22 µF; D1 only for large current.

equations.name: Maximum output current

where.η: power conversion efficiency of the converter

equations.note: For the worst case take the lowest input voltage, the highest output voltage and the minimum current limit. With 70 % efficiency at 0.9 V in, the 2.2 V example gives 114 mA.

equations.name: Switching frequency in continuous conduction
equations.expr: fSW = VIN × (VOUT − VIN × η) / (L × ILH × VOUT)
equations.note: fSW is not fixed: it moves with inductance, ripple current, input and output voltage.

equations.name: Continuous or discontinuous conduction
equations.expr: VOUT × IOUT / (VIN × η) > ILH / 2  →  continuous conduction
equations.note: If the left side is the smaller, the converter runs discontinuous.

equations.name: Peak inductor current, continuous conduction
equations.note: The 2.2 V, 50 mA example at 0.9 V and 80 % efficiency gives 258 mA. The 5 V, 500 mA example at 3 V and 90 % efficiency, with 500 mA ripple in 2.2 µH, gives 1.18 A.

operation.text: A synchronous boost converter with hysteretic current control, drawing 6.5 µA into VOUT, for alkaline, NiMH, Li-ion or Li-polymer cells. It is meant to stay on all the time. It starts from 0.9 V and, once running, keeps working with the input down to 0.4 V. The output is fixed inside the chip, 1.8 V to 5.5 V in 0.1 V steps, so only an inductor and an output capacitor are needed. Efficiency passes 90 % at 10 mA for 1.5 V in and 2.2 V out.

At power-up the high-side FET is on, so current flows from the input through the inductor and that FET into the output capacitors. Switching begins at a fixed 1.6 MHz once VOUT reaches about 0.83 V, and the high-side FET is then turned off. Above about 1.6 V out the reference ramps to 0.8 V within 2 ms, which keeps inrush current down. Soft start ends when the output is at its target; from then on the error amplifier output sets the inductor peak current.

The inductor ripple is held at about 200 mA and the output is regulated by moving the level of that ripple with load. An internal divider feeds the error amplifier, which compares it with the reference and sets the current offset. When the load needs less average current than the fixed ripple gives, the inductor current goes discontinuous, which keeps light-load efficiency high.

A Schottky diode from SW to VOUT raises the load the converter can carry: more than 500 mA at 5 V out, for USB OTG or HDMI supplies; the TPS613222A gives more than 500 mA from 3 V to 5 V this way. With the diode fitted, a constant-off-time circuit, adaptive, turns the high-side FET off and the inductor ripple grows past 200 mA; more inductance brings it down.
With the output above 1.8 V, the converter stops if the input falls below about 0.4 V. It switches again only when the input climbs back to 0.5 V (100 mV hysteresis).

Peak current is limited every cycle: when the inductor current reaches ILIM the low-side MOSFET switches off. In overload the output voltage sags until input and output power are equal. Once the output is below the input, the inductor current is held only by the inductor's DCR and the high-side MOSFET's on-resistance.
An on-chip sensor watches junction temperature while boosting. Above 150 °C the device stops; it restarts once the junction cools by the 20 °C hysteresis, to about 130 °C.
Continuous or discontinuous inductor current under the hysteretic control; protection by current limit, undervoltage lockout and overtemperature shutdown.

Three inductor figures matter: inductance, DC resistance and saturation current. Values from 0.7 µH to 13 µH work. The switching frequency depends on inductance; a smaller inductor ramps faster, and because the current comparator responds with some delay, the ripple gets larger. A larger inductor lowers the peak current. Inductor and output capacitor set the loop's bandwidth and phase margin together, so a larger inductor needs a larger capacitor to hold the L-to-C ratio. 4.7 µH is the choice for best stability at 2.2 V out. In the 2.2 V example the converter runs continuous, the peak is 258 mA, and a 4.7 µH part rated at least 300 mA saturation is chosen; 10 µH also works with more than 22 µF out. The inductor's saturation current must exceed the calculated peak, or the excess current harms the device. In the 5 V Schottky example a 2.2 µH part of at least 1.4 A saturation is chosen.

Use small low-ESR X5R or X7R ceramics at VOUT, placed tight against the VOUT and GND pins, to hold down the spike on SW. The device tolerates a -0.7 V negative spike on SW lasting up to 1 ns; deeper spikes can damage the internal MOSFET. If large capacitors must sit away from the device, put a 1 µF ceramic in parallel, right at the VOUT and GND pins. With 4.7 µH the minimum for stability is 10 µF effective; more capacitance lowers ripple. Allow for ceramic capacitance loss under DC bias. The 2.2 V example uses two GRM188R60J106ME84D 10 µF parts in parallel; the 5 V Schottky example uses three.

The fast switching calls for a fast rectifier. The diode's average and peak current ratings must exceed the peak inductor current and the mean output current, and its reverse breakdown voltage must exceed the highest output voltage. When D1 is fitted, an R1-C2 snubber is required; C2 must be more than three times the diode's capacitance. Typical values are R1 = 5 Ω and C2 = 120 pF.

The chip has no enable pin; it is cut off by an external switch Q1 between the battery and the converter. Q1 can be mechanical, needing no control logic, or else a PNP transistor or P-channel MOSFET. With an MCU, the GPIO drives the P-channel gate directly when the MCU supply is at least the battery voltage (Figure 8-21); when it is lower, an N-channel MOSFET between the gate and ground does the driving (Figure 8-22).
Input from 0.9 V to 5.5 V: alkaline, NiMH, Li-Mn or rechargeable Li-ion cells. The source has to be well regulated and inside the device's ratings.

High peak currents and fast switching make layout critical: a poor one gives instability and EMI. Keep the power ground paths and main current path short and wide, with inductor and output capacitor close to the device. Big ground planes on both top and bottom layers help thermal performance. The example layouts put the output capacitor straight across VOUT and GND and the inductor from VIN to SW, next to the chip.
